newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Corr looks ahead to new trial.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Corr looks ahead to new trial.

text.p: Cor Therapeutics Inc is looking ahead to another major trial of its flagship drug, hoping the result will mark a comeback for the biotechnology company.
Cor fell out of favor with many on Wall Street last year after a disappointing trial result for its blood-clot fighting drug Integrilin.
Cor and its partner Schering-Plough Corp expect to have results from its so-called Pursuit trial next summer, Cor Chief Executive Vaughn Kailian said in an interview Tuesday.
The interview was given during the American Heart Association's annual scientific sessions in New Orleans.
The Pursuit study is testing Integrilin in 11,000 patients for treating unstable angina, sharp chest pain that is often a sign of an oncoming heart attack, and some types of heart attacks.

Cor's stock has been in the doldrums since June 1995, when the company released results of a pivotal trial using Integrilin in conjunction with coronary angioplasty, a procedure in which a tiny balloon is used to widen a partially blocked blood vessel.
The company's stock dropped to about 10 from 19 after it said the data from the trial "did not achieve conventional statistical significance."
The stock was up 1/8 at 9-3/4 in Nasdaq trading at 1515 EST/2015 GMT Tuesday.

In April, Cor filed with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for approval of Integrilin's use in angioplasty. However, analysts said they viewed the Pursuit trial as the drug's make-it-or-break-it opportunity.
Cor "is a classic dark horse," said Josephthal, Lyon and Ross biotech analyst Franklin Berger.
Cor has argued that doses in the first trial were too small to be effective. The size of the doses were kept small because of concerns about possible bleeding brought on by the clot-busting drug.
Kailian said doses in the Pursuit trial are four times larger than in the first trial.
The target patient group in the Pursuit trial also represents the lion's share of the potential market for powerful anti-blood clot drugs, which include Centocor Inc's and Eli Lilly and Co's ReoPro.
"This trial will cover about 60 percent of the total market for these drugs," Kailian said.
Kailian said that an additional FDA filing based on the Pursuit data could come about four months after disclosure of the trial's results.
But analysts noted that even if the second trial goes well, Integrilin will have an uphill fight against ReoPro, which has been on the U.S. market since early 1995.

ReoPro was given a boost at the heart association conference from a study that showed the drug maintained its effectiveness in reducing deaths and heart attacks in angioplasty patients six months after the procedure.
